title.full: Just Energy Transition Partnership Indonesia, Comprehensive Investment and Policy Plan 2023

publisher.full: Indonesia Just Energy Transition Partnership Secretariat

description: Power transition strategy driven by managed coal phasedown and renewables scale-up.
pathwayDescription:
The Indonesia JETP Comprehensive Investment and Policy Plan (CIPP) outlines a conditional decarbonization pathway for the Indonesian power sector. Developed under the Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP), it defines the targets, investment requirements, and enabling policies needed to meet Indonesia’s stated energy transition goals. The CIPP is a non-binding strategy document that does not model a global temperature outcome, but it does provide quantitative benchmarks for Indonesia’s transition to a net-zero power system.

The pathway outlines a rapid pace of power grid transition, with renewables rising to 44% of on-grid generation by 2030. The pathway limits grid emissions to 250 Mt by 2030, with continued significant declines through 2050.

investmentNeeds.value: By tech, part of value chain

coreDrivers.policies: Policies are reformed to support renewables scaling and coal phased down. RE/VRE target shares and phaseout/early retirement targets are embedded. Market-policy drivers: LCR reform, bankable PPAs/procurement and removal of coal price distortions are policy enablers.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: The pathway uses an on-grid CO2 emissions cap of 250 Mt in 2030, a reduction to 175 Mt by 2040, and near net-zero emissions by 2050. This is a central normative constraint.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Technology-level costs drive the least-cost supply optimization and support the modeled build-out of low-carbon generation. Falling utility-scale solar PV and onshore wind LCOE make these technologies the least expensive new generation options by 2030.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Technology-level costs drive the least-cost supply optimization and support the modeled build-out of low-carbon generation. Falling utility-scale solar PV and onshore wind LCOE make these technologies the least expensive new generation options by 2030.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Estimates from the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources point to 6% GDP growth p.a. until 2030, 7% p.a. from 2030 to 2040, and then a convergence to high income countries between 2040 and 2050, while the population is estimated to grow from 276 mio. in 2022 to 324 mio. in 2050. Electricity demand growth is an important inpu in the JETP, with an assumed 6.0% annual demand growth including captive connections.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Grid integration and system flexibility are major additional drivers: transmission follows RUPTL to 2030, large-island interconnection starts from 2029, coal flexible utilization is explicitly included, and storage grows to 38 GW by 2050. Captive load connections affect demand, while captive generation decarbonization is planned separately.

dependencies.dependency_description: The pathway depends on a policy package to enable grid decarbonization and coal phase-down, including an emissions cap, RE/VRE share targets, early coal retirement/managed phase-out, LCR reform, procurement/PPA reform, PLN financial sustainability and financial-policy support. These policies are intended to lower renewable costs, expose coal's true cost and make renewable procurement/investment bankable.

Regulatory reform is a binding enabler for renewable procurement and coal phase-out. The pathway calls for LCR reform, competitive procurement, bankable PPAs, legal clarity for early retirement and flexible coal use and captive power decarbonization. THese regulatory reforms affect pace and financeability of renewables scale up and coal phase-out.

The JETP agreement includes US$ 20bn in required investments, half of which are committed through public funding and half of which are meant to be privately finacned. A GFANZ working group including international financial institutions aims to mobilize that private capital and the expected financing structures are manifold from plain public and private financing instruments, to blended finance and philantropic grants.

The pathway treats just transition and equitable risk/opportunity sharing as necessary for implementation, especially for communities and workers affected by coal phase-out and project deployment, but does not quantify the impacts in detail.

The pathway outcome depends on power transmission/distribution expansion, large-island interconnections, grid-scale energy storage and operational flexibility to integrate 38 GW variable RE by 2030 and 309 GW by 2050. It identifies grid forecasting, merit-order dispatch, new substations and transmission capacity, energy storage and ancillary services, demand response, and digitalization as required over time.

Technology readiness/deployment is material for storage, solar/wind scale-up, nuclear, and later low-carbon fuels for repurposed coal/gas plants. Hydrogen-based fuels grow to 81.4 TWh generation and 31.4 GW capacity by 2050, while aggregate storage reaches 38 GW. Both are currently non-existent on the Indonesian energy mix.

Labor/skills and job-transition needs are relevant because coal phase-down and renewable supply-chain development affect employment. Additional investment is projected to create over 400000 new jobs by 2030, but the CIPP acknowledges that phaseout of coal power will requrie re-skilling programs to cushion the impact of job losses in that area.
